doc-start.0: AIDE is a desktop code editor with an AI studio built in: an agent, a design canvas and a team of twelve roles work in one window. Below is the short path from install to your first edit.
doc-start.5: Describe the task in the chat on the right. The agent proposes a plan, asks permission for file writes and commands, and reports what it did together with the token count.
doc-start.6: If you just use the installer, Node.js and Rust are not needed — everything is already inside.
doc-install.2: The ready-made installer is on this site: the “Download for Windows” button in the Start section. You need Windows 10 or 11 and WebView2 — current builds already have it.
doc-install.3: [b]Building from source.[/b] [code]npm install[/code], then [code]npm run tauri build[/code]. The files land in the [code]bundle[/code] folder next to the project: an NSIS installer and an MSI package.
doc-install.4: [b]Updates arrive by themselves.[/b] Once a day AIDE compares its version with the latest GitHub release and offers to update. You can also check manually.
doc-install.5: [b]Signature.[/b] Update files are checked against a cryptographic signature: the app will not trust a build from an outside source.
doc-install.6: [b]Windows warning.[/b] The installer is not signed with a paid publisher certificate, so SmartScreen may ask for confirmation on first launch. It does not affect the editor itself.
doc-install.7: [b]Uninstalling.[/b] The usual Windows uninstall. Your projects, settings and keys stay in place — remove them separately if you want to.
doc-workspace.2: The project tree is on the left. Files and folders are created, renamed and deleted from the context menu, and changes on disk are picked up right away: an outside edit is never lost.
doc-workspace.3: [b]Tabs.[/b] They keep their cursor position and undo history and close with the middle mouse button. Images, PDFs and fonts open for preview right in the editor.
doc-workspace.4: [b]Panels.[/b] Explorer, project search, Git, snippets and extensions switch in the left panel and stay out of each other's way.
doc-workspace.5: [b]Text search.[/b] [kbd]Ctrl[/kbd]+[kbd]Shift[/kbd]+[kbd]F[/kbd] searches by text, with case and file masks.
doc-workspace.6: [b]Search by meaning.[/b] A query like “parse config file” finds the right places even when the code uses other words: function and path names count separately from plain text.
doc-workspace.7: [b]Command palette.[/b] [kbd]Ctrl[/kbd]+[kbd]P[/kbd] — files and actions without the mouse.
doc-editor.2: The editor is built on CodeMirror 6: highlighting, line numbers, completion, search and replace, multiple cursors and folding.
doc-editor.3: [b]Language servers.[/b] Type hints, error squiggles, go to definition and back, rename a symbol and format a file — the same servers VS Code uses.
doc-editor.4: [b]Works without a server.[/b] If no language server is installed for a language, highlighting, navigation and symbol search remain.
doc-editor.5: [b]Git conflicts.[/b] Shown as a merge view: accept your side or theirs with a button, no need to edit the file by hand.
doc-editor.6: [b]Agent edits.[/b] [kbd]Ctrl[/kbd]+[kbd]K[/kbd] on selected code — the agent proposes a new version and you accept or reject it by diff.
doc-chat.2: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and any compatible server are supported: the address and the model list are set in the provider settings.
doc-chat.3: [b]Local models.[/b] Ollama or LM Studio on this computer — then requests never leave the machine.
doc-chat.4: [b]Keys.[/b] Stored in the Windows Credential Manager, separately per provider. A key never reaches the project, the model's reply or a log.
doc-chat.5: [b]Tokens.[/b] Every answer shows what it cost, so models can be compared by price rather than by feel.
doc-chat.6: [b]History.[/b] Lives in the project: come back to the folder and the conversation continues where it stopped.
doc-chat.7: [b]Attachments.[/b] Attach a file or an image to a message and its text joins the model's context.
doc-chat.8: [b]Queue.[/b] If the agent is still working, a new message waits in the queue; the arrow next to it sends it immediately and stops the current answer.
doc-agent.6: [b]Clarifications.[/b] When a task can be read in different ways, the agent asks first and then works — it does not decide for you.
doc-term.2: [b]A real pty.[/b] Interactive programs, colours, arrows and [kbd]Ctrl[/kbd]+[kbd]C[/kbd] all work. As many terminal tabs as you need.
doc-term.3: [b]Git panel.[/b] Changed files, a line-by-line diff, branch and history; commits are made from there too.
doc-term.4: [b]Agent commands.[/b] It can run them, but only with your confirmation: you see exactly what is about to run.
doc-checks.2: [b]After edits.[/b] AIDE runs the project's checks — types, linter, tests — and reports back if something broke.
doc-checks.3: [b]Before “done”.[/b] The verify-before-done skill requires re-reading the diff, building the project and running the tests.
doc-checks.4: [b]Diagnostics.[/b] Language server errors show up in the panel immediately, before the project is even run.
doc-checks.5: [b]Turning off.[/b] Self-checks can be disabled in settings when a project is big and the checks take long.
doc-rules.3: Project rules beat the agent's habits: if a file forbids changing something, the agent asks instead of doing it silently.
doc-safe.2: [b]Keys.[/b] In the Windows Credential Manager. Not in the project, the repository or the logs.
doc-safe.3: [b]Permissions.[/b] File writes, commands and network access only after confirmation.
doc-safe.4: [b]Your code.[/b] Stays on disk: AIDE sends it only to the model you chose.
doc-safe.5: [b]A local model.[/b] Then nothing leaves the computer at all.
doc-safe.6: [b]No telemetry.[/b] The app collects no usage statistics and sends no hidden reports.
doc-settings.2: [b]Appearance.[/b] Interface language, theme, editor font size, panel and terminal behaviour.
doc-settings.3: [b]Providers.[/b] A fixed model list for servers that cannot list models themselves.
doc-settings.4: [b]Skills.[/b] Built-in rule sets can be switched on and off: verify before done, careful changes, secure code, debugging, tests, frontend.
doc-settings.5: [b]Permissions.[/b] What the agent may do without asking and what always needs a confirmation.
doc-faq.2: Do I need Node.js and Rust just to use AIDE?
doc-faq.3: No. The installer already contains everything the app needs. Node is only needed for checks in your own project, and Rust only if you build AIDE yourself.
doc-faq.5: Only to the model you chose. With a local model it goes nowhere.
doc-faq.7: In the Windows Credential Manager, encrypted, separately for each provider.
doc-faq.9: Yes, with a local model: the editor, terminal and Git always work, and the agent works with the local model.
doc-faq.10: What if the agent makes a mistake?
doc-faq.11: A checkpoint is taken before edits and Undo restores the files. Permissions stop it from doing anything without your consent.
doc-faq.12: Does AIDE run on macOS or Linux?
doc-faq.13: The build is for Windows today. The Tauri and React code is portable, but there are no ready builds for other systems.
doc-faq.15: By itself: the app checks for an update and offers to install it. Or download the new installer from this site.
doc-faq.16: Why does Windows warn when installing?
doc-faq.17: The installer is not signed with a paid publisher certificate — that is a SmartScreen warning, not a virus. Update signatures are verified separately.
doc-fix.2: [b]The model does not answer.[/b] Check the key and the provider address in settings and your internet access. Error 401 means a wrong key, 429 means a rate limit.
doc-fix.3: [b]It will not install.[/b] Close the running AIDE and try again.
doc-fix.4: [b]Panels disappeared.[/b] [kbd]Ctrl[/kbd]+[kbd]B[/kbd] and [kbd]Ctrl[/kbd]+[kbd]J[/kbd] bring back the side panel and the terminal.
doc-fix.5: [b]The terminal is empty.[/b] Open a new terminal tab — the old session may have ended.
doc-fix.6: [b]No highlighting or hints.[/b] A language server may be missing for that language: install it in the system and the editor picks it up.
doc-fix.7: [b]Checks fail.[/b] Paste the check output into the chat — the agent reads the error and fixes the cause, not the symptom.

t-code.2: The app claims no rights to your code. Everything you write, edit and generate in AIDE stays yours — including code the agent produced for your task.
t-code.3: Projects live on your disk. AIDE does not upload them to its own storage and keeps no cloud copies. What exactly leaves the machine when a model is called is described in the Privacy policy.
t-models.2: The agent needs a model to work. With an external model the request goes to that provider's servers and is handled under their rules. The author does not control those servers and is not responsible for their availability.
t-models.3: [b]Payment.[/b] You pay the provider directly for requests at their rates. AIDE takes no commission on tokens and issues no token invoices.
t-models.4: [b]A local model.[/b] With a model on the same computer, requests never leave the machine.
t-models.5: [b]Model answers.[/b] Generated text can be wrong. The app shows it as a proposal, not as a fact, and you make the decision.

privacy-title.2: What AIDE does with your data, what it keeps on the computer, what it sends over the network and when — and what it never does.
p-sum.2: The app collects no telemetry and keeps no usage statistics.
p-sum.3: Your code stays on your disk.
p-sum.4: Only a request to the model you chose leaves the machine — and only if that model is external.
p-sum.5: Access keys live in the protected Windows store, not in project files.
p-who.2: AIDE and the site that distributes it are run by the project author, Abubakr Sanginov. He decides which data the app needs and is responsible for protecting it within his means.
p-who.3: Processing mostly happens on your computer. The app has no server side: there is no account and no server that would keep your projects.
p-none.2: No telemetry and no usage analytics: the app sends no reports about what you opened or which buttons you pressed.
p-none.3: No contents of your projects, files or agent conversations to our servers — there are no such servers.
p-none.4: No list of installed programs, file names or browser history.
p-none.5: No advertising identifiers or advertising profiles.
p-local.1: What is stored on the computer
p-local.2: Everything the app needs to work lives locally:
p-local.4: In the folders you opened. The app writes there only on your command or with your permission.
p-local.6: In the app's data folder in your Windows profile: theme, language, font size, provider list, conversation history per project.
p-local.8: In the Windows Credential Manager, one record per provider. Project files never contain them.
p-local.10: Checkpoints taken before agent edits — temporary, used by the Undo button.
p-net.2: The only mandatory internet request is the call to the model you chose. It carries what you sent: the task text, attached files and the code or project fragments needed for the answer.
p-net.3: [b]To whom.[/b] To the model provider you configured: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google or your own server. From there, their policy and their rules apply.
p-net.4: [b]Update checks.[/b] The app reads the GitHub releases page to learn the number of the new version. That is a plain file request; project contents are not sent with it.
p-net.5: [b]Pages the agent asks for.[/b] If a task needs a page from the internet, the address goes to that site — just as if you opened it in a browser.
p-net.6: [b]Nothing beyond that.[/b] No background reports, counters or “anonymous statistics” are sent.
p-keys.2: An API key is a password to your account at a model provider. The app keeps it in the Windows Credential Manager, encrypted, separately for each provider.
p-keys.3: The key is not written into project files, does not reach a repository and is not printed in logs.
p-keys.4: The key is not forwarded to the model in the request text and is not shown in the interface after saving.
p-keys.5: A key can be deleted in settings — the record is erased from the store.
p-lm.2: If you connect a model running on this same computer (Ollama or LM Studio, for example), requests go to a local address and never leave the machine. In this mode the app can work entirely without internet — apart from the update check, which you may skip.
p-site.2: The site is static pages. It has no forms with personal data, no ad networks and no third-party counters: the pages' security policy forbids loading foreign scripts.
p-site.3: [b]Cookies.[/b] The site sets no tracking cookies. Page preferences, such as the lite mode, live in your browser's localStorage and are never sent anywhere.
p-site.4: [b]Hosting logs.[/b] The pages are hosted on Vercel. Like any host, it keeps technical request logs: page address, time, browser type, IP address. Those logs keep the site running and protected.
p-site.5: [b]Language.[/b] The page language comes from the address, not from a visitor profile.
p-dl.2: The installer is served from this site or from the GitHub releases page. While downloading, the host and GitHub see the ordinary technical data of a request. The installer contains no built-in counters and sends no installation report.
p-share.2: We do not sell or share data with third parties, because we do not hold it. Technical site data is handled by the host, and model requests by the provider you chose; each follows its own rules.
p-keep.2: Data on your computer is kept until you delete it: settings until the app is uninstalled, chat history until you clear it in the interface or delete the data folder, keys until you delete them in settings. Technical site logs are kept by the host for its standard period.
p-rights.2: Since processing mostly happens on your device, you control the data yourself: you can view, change and delete settings, history and keys at any time. If you believe processing violates your rights, write through the project page on GitHub — the request will be considered on its merits.
p-sec.2: Traffic to external services goes over an encrypted connection.
p-sec.3: Updates are verified by cryptographic signature — a swapped file will not be installed.
p-sec.4: File writes, terminal commands and network access happen only after your confirmation.
p-sec.5: A checkpoint is taken before edits, so changes can be undone.
p-kids.2: The app is meant for developers and is not addressed to children. We deliberately collect no data about children — in fact we collect no personal data through the app at all.
p-change.2: The policy may be updated together with the app: for example, if a new feature that uses the network appears. The current revision is always on this page with the date at the top. Material changes are noted in the changelog.
p-contact.2: Questions about data and privacy: the project page on GitHub, in the issues section. The author and the data controller is Abubakr Sanginov.
p-contact.3: This page describes how data is handled and is not legal advice.
doc-crew.3: You are the CEO: you decide what of it makes it into the code.
